title: Imatinib for gastrointestinal stromal tumour (GIST)
context_label: KIT-positive gastrointestinal stromal tumour (GIST): unresectable/metastatic treatment or adjuvant treatment after resection
indication_text: KIT-positive gastrointestinal stromal tumour (GIST): unresectable/metastatic treatment or adjuvant treatment after resection
purpose: For unresectable or metastatic gastrointestinal stromal tumour (GIST), imatinib aims to control disease and symptoms. After removal of higher-risk GIST, adjuvant treatment aims to reduce the chance of recurrence. These are different treatment goals and must be clearly recorded.
schedule_label: Imatinib every day; no routine break
schedule_summary: The usual National Cancer Control Programme starting dose is 400 mg by mouth every day with food. For progression in advanced disease, a specialist may consider 800 mg daily as 400 mg twice daily. Adjuvant treatment after resection is described as up to 3 years in this National Cancer Control Programme document; your specialist confirms duration using current risk and evidence. The 28-day graphic is a reference view, not a treatment break or fixed course.
administration_text: Take the prescribed dose with a meal and a large glass of water. Take doses consistently. If swallowing is difficult, ask the pharmacy about the exact supplied product before changing how it is taken.
monitoring_summary: Use the test-specific schedule below. Safety blood tests and tumour/recurrence scans have different purposes.

agents.name: Imatinib
agents.type: Oral targeted therapy: tyrosine kinase inhibitor
agents.explanation: Imatinib blocks certain kinase proteins, including KIT and platelet-derived growth factor receptor alpha, that can drive susceptible gastrointestinal stromal tumour (GIST) cells. The exact tumour mutation affects sensitivity; a KIT-positive label alone does not replace specialist molecular review. Normal tissues can also be affected.
agents.watch: Report rapid weight gain, swelling, new breathlessness, fever, unusual bleeding, severe rash or yellow eyes promptly. Keep blood tests even if you feel well.
risks: Nausea, diarrhoea, abdominal discomfort, fatigue, muscle cramps and rash
Swelling around the eyes or elsewhere; occasionally severe fluid retention or heart failure
Low blood counts with infection, anaemia or bleeding
Liver injury, occasionally severe; kidney function may decline with treatment
Rare severe skin reactions, gastrointestinal bleeding or perforation, hepatitis B reactivation and small-vessel clotting that can injure blood cells and kidneys
Fertility or pregnancy harm; discuss product-specific contraception and breastfeeding

anatomy: Tiredness, muscle cramps or weakness can affect daily activity. Report new or severe symptoms; do not assume all weakness is ordinary fatigue.
Nausea or mouth symptoms can affect eating and drinking. Ask for practical symptom support early.
Rapid weight gain, new swelling or breathlessness may indicate fluid retention and needs prompt assessment.
Regular blood tests detect liver effects. Report yellow eyes, dark urine or significant abdominal pain urgently.
Kidney function is monitored during treatment. Report reduced urine, marked swelling or difficulty drinking.
Low counts can cause infection, anaemia or bleeding. Fever, chills or sudden illness requires immediate oncology contact.
Report persistent diarrhoea. Severe abdominal pain, black stools or other significant bleeding needs urgent assessment.
Rash can occur. Widespread blistering, peeling skin or mouth/eye involvement needs urgent help.

monitoring_schedule.note: Safety testing and tumour/recurrence assessment answer different questions.

monitoring_test_details.label: Full blood count
monitoring_test_details.purpose: Check infection-fighting cells, oxygen-carrying red cells and platelets.
monitoring_test_details.timing: At baseline, every 2 weeks for the first 12 weeks, then monthly; extra testing may be needed for symptoms or abnormal results.

monitoring_test_details.label: Kidney and liver tests
monitoring_test_details.purpose: Detect organ effects and review safe treatment.
monitoring_test_details.timing: At baseline, then monthly; repeat sooner for abnormal results, dehydration, swelling or other clinical concerns.

monitoring_test_details.label: Hepatitis B screening and follow-up
monitoring_test_details.purpose: Detect infection that can reactivate during treatment.
monitoring_test_details.timing: Screen before treatment. Positive results require specialist advice and individual monitoring during treatment and for months afterwards.

monitoring_test_details.label: Heart, weight and fluid review
monitoring_test_details.purpose: Detect fluid retention or cardiac problems.
monitoring_test_details.timing: Baseline electrocardiogram (heart tracing) and review of heart/kidney history; monitor weight, swelling and breathlessness during treatment. Additional heart tests are clinically directed.

monitoring_test_details.label: Thyroid testing in a specific setting
monitoring_test_details.purpose: Check whether thyroid replacement remains appropriate.
monitoring_test_details.timing: Check thyroid-stimulating hormone when indicated, particularly after thyroid removal in someone taking levothyroxine. This is not a universal monthly thyroid test.

monitoring_test_details.label: Tumour or recurrence review
monitoring_test_details.purpose: Assess benefit separately from treatment-safety tests.
monitoring_test_details.timing: Your gastrointestinal stromal tumour (GIST) specialist sets imaging and clinical-review timing. Adjuvant recurrence monitoring and advanced-disease response assessment are different plans.

support.title: Preparation and support medicines
support.text: Confirm whether treatment is for advanced disease or after surgery, and the exact daily dose. Review all prescribed, over-the-counter and herbal products; avoid grapefruit and St John’s wort. Never increase the dose after a scan or a missed dose without the team. A routine tablet break, growth factor or steroid course is not part of this schedule. Nausea prevention depends partly on dose: the National Cancer Control Programme oral emetogenic category changes above 400 mg/day. Use the individually prescribed symptom plan and report persistent diarrhoea, vomiting or swelling. Hepatitis B follow-up is individualised if screening is positive.

support.title: Oral medicine handling
support.text: Keep tablets or capsules in their supplied packaging, away from children, and follow the pharmacy storage instructions. Do not share medicines or alter the dose yourself. Ask the pharmacy before crushing, opening or dispersing a medicine; formulation-specific instructions differ. Return unused treatment to the pharmacy.

support.title: Fertility and pregnancy precautions
support.text: Discuss fertility, effective contraception, pregnancy prevention and breastfeeding before treatment. Your team must give the product-specific precautions and duration for you and your partner. Tell oncology promptly about a possible pregnancy.

support.title: Your wider treatment plan
support.text: gastrointestinal stromal tumour (GIST) is a distinct tumour type. A specialist team reviews pathology, KIT/platelet-derived growth factor receptor alpha and other relevant molecular findings, prior treatment, symptoms and scans. Surgery may be appropriate for resectable disease or selected situations. Radiotherapy has a selective role, rather than being a routine partner to these tablets. Nutrition, symptom control and supportive or palliative care can be used alongside active cancer treatment.

support.title: Missed or vomited doses
support.text: If you miss an imatinib dose, take it when remembered unless it is nearly time for the next dose; then skip it and return to the usual schedule. Never double a dose. Ask the team what to do after vomiting; do not take a replacement dose without advice.

evidence.title: SSGXVIII/AIO: three versus one year of adjuvant imatinib
evidence.summary: An early study in advanced gastrointestinal stromal tumour (GIST) demonstrated tumour responses and disease control with imatinib; it was not an adjuvant study. Separately, in high-risk GIST after surgery, three years of adjuvant imatinib improved recurrence-free and overall survival compared with one year at long follow-up. Keep these treatment settings distinct.
evidence.intro: An early study in advanced gastrointestinal stromal tumour (GIST) demonstrated tumour responses and disease control with imatinib; it was not an adjuvant study. Separately, in high-risk GIST after surgery, three years of adjuvant imatinib improved recurrence-free and overall survival compared with one year at long follow-up. Keep these treatment settings distinct.
evidence.caveat: The National Cancer Control Programme document describes up to three years after surgery. Later IMADGIST evidence supports disease-free survival benefit from extending treatment in selected high-risk patients, so three years should not be labelled universally optimal or imposed as an automatic stop. Advanced gastrointestinal stromal tumour (GIST) requires its own evidence and continuation discussion.

questions.q: What is the treatment trying to do?
questions.a: For unresectable or metastatic gastrointestinal stromal tumour (GIST), imatinib aims to control disease and symptoms. After removal of higher-risk GIST, adjuvant treatment aims to reduce the chance of recurrence. These are different treatment goals and must be clearly recorded. GIST is a distinct tumour type. A specialist team reviews pathology, KIT/platelet-derived growth factor receptor alpha and other relevant molecular findings, prior treatment, symptoms and scans. Surgery may be appropriate for resectable disease or selected situations. Radiotherapy has a selective role, rather than being a routine partner to these tablets. Nutrition, symptom control and supportive or palliative care can be used alongside active cancer treatment.

The usual National Cancer Control Programme starting dose is 400 mg by mouth every day with food. For progression in advanced disease, a specialist may consider 800 mg daily as 400 mg twice daily. Adjuvant treatment after resection is described as up to 3 years in this National Cancer Control Programme document; your specialist confirms duration using current risk and evidence. The 28-day graphic is a reference view, not a treatment break or fixed course.

questions.q: Does a delay mean treatment has failed?
questions.a: No. Blood counts, organ function and symptoms can make a delay or dose change safer. Your team decides whether and when to give the next dose.

questions.q: Who do I contact if unwell?
questions.a: Use your verified oncology daytime or out-of-hours number. If you cannot reach the team, seek urgent medical assessment. Severe symptoms require 112/999.

questions.q: What should I do about a missed or vomited dose?
questions.a: If you miss an imatinib dose, take it when remembered unless it is nearly time for the next dose; then skip it and return to the usual schedule. Never double a dose. Ask the team what to do after vomiting; do not take a replacement dose without advice.

questions.q: Can I take other medicines or supplements?
questions.a: Confirm whether treatment is for advanced disease or after surgery, and the exact daily dose. Review all prescribed, over-the-counter and herbal products; avoid grapefruit and St John’s wort. Never increase the dose after a scan or a missed dose without the team.

questions.q: Why do I need checks if I feel well?
questions.a: High blood pressure, thyroid changes, liver injury or low blood counts may be detected before you notice symptoms. The required checks differ by medicine; keep your individual schedule.
